pages.label: 002_Louis Armstrong and Herman Chittison Interview, 1960-05-04 Part 2

blocks.x: Neil, I was going through some books here that I wanted to ask you about, some early recordings and all, but before I did that, I wanted to ask you about some mundane facts about yourself, you know, about your birth date and where you were born and all that kind of stuff. I was born on the south side. Here in Atlanta? In Atlanta, Georgia. Native son. Yeah. On the Capitol Avenue. What was your part of you? Capitol Avenue? Near Capitol Avenue, the Creekmont Sanitarium. And that is considered a historic part of town. It was a mixture, a dukes mixture as far as the neighborhood is concerned. You mean low-income groups? Yeah, heritage genius. The most rural, most of us were rural. And then part of the town in that section had, it was a Jewish neighborhood. And I got most of that work later on when I got up, pretty well known. From that group of people? From that group of people. From that group of people. For parties and all that. Yeah. And they had a Jewish alliance, not so far from the neighborhood, in which a number of them, the fellows there, they began to go into clubs. Right now, out here on, out on Tech, it's a Jewish regressive club. I think I've seen that. You've seen it. Yeah, I did. It's at 10th Street. And most of those fellows have gravitated into that club there. They have membership in that club. And they belong to the club. But it has its roots back there on Capitol Avenue, where I was born. And those fellows are still, for a long time, used me in connection with their social affairs. See, so it tied in very neatly. Well, this was, it was not mostly Negro and Jewish then. Negro and Jewish, and Jewish, it was a Negro and Jewish neighborhood. That's the part that's now torn down over there. That's the part torn over there. And part of it has been rebuilt over there by Georgia Tech. Yeah. You see? So, it tied in very well with my social affairs and with the business. Sooner or later, it did that. And finally, after a while, in the course of time, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they began to get older themselves. And naturally, they began to raise their children, their families, and like that. And things began to taper off then. But it was a, it was a, it was a, it was a, it was a, it was a social, social of my business. For a long time. Most years. And, and, and I was, it really, it was a, I was amused. I, I dug, I dug tail, into one thing, dug tail into another. The early contacts. Yeah, early contacts, one of the set, that kind of, what is my business. Well, when were you born, Nick? What's your birth? 1903. What month? Uh, 363. 363. 1903. That makes you 61, right? 61. Right. Great. Most people have to, most people have to be under. Well, I don't have to, I don't have to, I don't have to, I don't have to, I don't have to, Oh, gee, you were very quick with it, huh? I can do that. Uh, something that simple. Uh, well, tell me what your parents did. What kind of, what kind of. My father, my father was an ardent member of the Methodist Church. What occupation did he have? He was a, he was a, he was a chemist. For a local firm here? For a local firm, yeah. And, uh, he learned how to mix the, uh, the things, uh, mix the, uh, the medicines and all like that. Uh, but by someone teaching him, and he kept it in his mind for, for, for, for, for, for five, fifty years. Hmm. He made the, help make the, uh, the medicine called Mother's Friend. You ever seen it? Mother's Friend. I've heard of that. Yeah. Mother's Friend. Still big. Still right now. Mother's Friend, and he made that. Well, what happened? Forty some odd years. Does he live in there? No, he passed. About ten years ago. Five, five, ten years ago. And, uh, he was a great singer. He was, uh, he was a, he wasn't a great singer, but he was, he, he was, uh, he liked to sing a lot. What, what kind of voice? He had bass, bass? Bass. And, and in an afternoon, in the, in every Sunday afternoon, he said, uh, Neil come on and play some music for me. And I played the music for that he would, he would, he would, he would ask me to play. My mother would sing soprano. So this is where you got your interest in music. So, so she, she sang soprano, and he sang the bass. And then I, I tried to sing a little tenor, and made a quartet out of it, you know. Well, this is later on that you did this. No, this is in the early days. Were you doing this in the early days? The real early? The early days. And up to about, uh, until I got about 21. And then, uh, after that, uh, uh, we getting to, well, my interest began to weigh in. And, uh, what kind of stuff did you play in the home when you were small? Religious music. Religious music. Nothing but religious music. I could, I played anything I wanted to play. But he liked to hear me play religious music. And I play some of it now. Did you, when did you learn to play the piano? How did you learn to play the piano? I learned to play the piano when I was around about six or seven years of age. By yourself? I had a dad instructor. The lady who taught me in the second grade, in the first grade or second grade. She came to the home? No, she came to the home. And, uh, Did you want to learn or was it something you learned? I did want to learn. I actually wanted to learn. And, uh, she had, uh, some, uh, she had, uh, had me to buy a book. What? The book was by, by Matthews. And it's a, the book is still being sold down the case, down through cable piano companies. Mr. Munn. Uh, he is the one who, he sells that book in case I, I have sometimes people who ask, let's keep on insisting. We want a music book, something to act as a guide. So I just call up Mr. Munn and tell him, give him that book. Because I like that book particularly, see. But, uh, it was, uh, Were you half people? I suppose you just took right off. Well, at that time, at that time, the fellas didn't play. I mean, the musicians, uh, there were not, there were, there were no musicians who, who, who, who read or studied. They just picked it up. Uh-huh. Just like, uh, just play for, like a fellow James Johnson, uh, playing, just just playing, just as such. But no one who would study. You say you learned about five or six years old to play? I learned when I was about six years of age. Well, now what kind of music did you hear at that time? Most were church music? Church music. Or semi-classical? Semi-classical. And church music. You didn't hear any, uh, street music or, uh, Didn't this kind of, They didn't have too much of it. Uh-huh. There wasn't a great, a great amount of it. There wasn't a great pollution. There was a lot of that time. Yeah. I, at nine being, uh, late on, when I got to the, uh, uh, tenth and eleventh and twelfth, then Fletcher Henderson came by, came to Atlanta. Uh, in other words, uh, you mean when you were, uh, Uh, you mean when he moved here? Yeah. And you all went to school together, right? Yeah, that's right. See, Fletcher was the most outstanding musician in town. You see, because, uh, he, he was studying. He was studying from a lady from a New England conservator who, who taught music in the college. And, uh, labeled high school. Well, this was actually a high school, was it not? The first, high school. It was high school first. That is, uh, he was in college. He was in, uh, Atlanta, which is now the Atlanta University. Yeah. It was then the Atlanta, it was still Atlanta University. Yeah, it was, it still was, it was always that university. But, of course, people make the distinction now. Uh, university is, uh, uh, you go one year beyond your college before you get into university. But, of course, they didn't make that distinction at the time, but they make the distinction now. Uh, by that time, he was in the college, because he hadn't graduated. And I was way down in high school, I guess, uh, eighth grade. Well, did you, uh, you became friends with him at that time? I became friends with him. You all played piano together? He would, yeah, that's right. He would, we'd have sessions. And there was a fellow named, who came along with us named Ford, who played like a player piano. And, uh, he would, I, I would play some, then, then this, uh, then Ford would play, then Fletcher would play. This was all when you were kids, at 12 and 13? Yeah, yeah, Fletcher was older. He was 20, 20, or 21. Oh, was he that much older? Yeah, he was much older than that, yeah. Yeah, I would talk about. Well, I see, well then, uh, then he was out of school and playing the band here, then, wouldn't he? Well, no, I was in the band here. Yeah, everybody was, everybody was wanting to hear Fletcher, Fletcher play. Everybody expected him to play. Wherever there was a group of people, peers socially, they expected Fletcher to play. And then, oh, Fletcher would play for a while, an hour, then I'd play for an hour, and then I, then Ford would play for an hour, two hours, something like that. Then there was another young lady by the name of, um, Connie Berry. Connie Berry? Connie Berry. B-E-R-Y. Yeah. Now, wait, I want to go back a little bit. When was this with you and Ford and Fletcher were all playing? About, when was this? About how old were all of you then? 1920. It was 1921. This was before he went to New York. Because Fletcher would, yeah. He went to New York about 1920, 21. That's right. This was before he went to New York. Uh-huh. This was before he went to New York. He went there as a chemist, too, you know. Yeah, he did. He was beating the, his fellow named, a friend of his, named Pace. That's right. Pace Music Publishing. Yeah, that's right. He went there and was, uh, he was a musical director. He was a musical director, I understand, for the Pace. Black Swan Records. Black Swan Records, that's right. That's right. I, I've got a lot of those Black Swan Records. Yeah. Well, he was at, uh, well, he, he conducted the, the, uh, music for the Black Swan Records Company. And they finally, uh, went into other things. Yeah. Well, they went into, I think Columbia. Columbia, too. No, Paramount. Paramount. They sold Paramount by one day. Yeah. But that was the original race record they called then, a Negro. Yeah, it was. It was right. You're right. There was a great, uh, arranger that I can't remember his name now that was with Black Swan at the time. I wondered if you would remember him. But I can't think of his name now. Arranger? Yeah. Well known. Arranger. But I can't remember his name now at all. Uh, well, did you learn plenty of other instruments besides the piano? That was interesting. I started with the violin. Oh, you started with the violin. Yeah, I started with, I, I, I didn't make any progress with the violin. It wasn't enough to, to offset the piano. Now, earlier you were telling me about a piano player that you heard that really sort of set you afire and took you down from the classical and to the swinging jazz part. It was Harvey Twiggs. Harvey Twiggs. Harvey Twiggs. Harvey Twiggs. And, uh, do you remember about when this was, when you heard him? I heard him back there before, uh, that is before Fletcher Henderson left town. Was this after the First World War or? After the first, it was, uh, after the First World War. After the First World War. And because, uh, he ignited me. He was the first one to really have, which I considered to have swing. And he had a definite beat. He didn't have any drum, bass, violin, and, he just had a good beat that I liked. And I tried to imitate it. Uh-huh. You say he sounded very much like James P. Oh, I just liked him. Real strong. Couldn't tell the difference. It's a pity he didn't record, isn't it? It is. He supposed to be. It was too bad that he, he didn't, uh, it was too bad that he didn't, his schooling was short-lived. He went to, he didn't go any further than the seventh, eighth grade. Well, how, how long did he play on the local scene here? He played no longer than about four or five years. I wonder what happened to him. I don't know what happened. He just, just went off the scene. See, fellas would come, come, come, come in, and all of a sudden they'd disappear. They'd disappear. I don't know what happened. I'm gonna look in the book here and see if I see Harvey Twigs. Harvey Twigs. Harvey Twigs. He never did record anything, as I know, as I remember. Harvey Twigs. He had, had a beat. T-W-I-G-G-U. That's right. I, I know where his house is, where he lives, and where he lives. I don't see his name here now. No, must not have. Well, a lot of people like that didn't record that were good. Yeah, they were good. It's a shame that . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . As long as anybody around here remembers, just about it. How did you come about doing this, Neil? When did you do it, and when was the first band and some of the... It was during the... It was the lady who was Oberlin graduate, encouraged me to... Oberlin graduate. And she was... She wanted... She liked jazz music. And of course she played nothing but classics. You were... Were I school at this time? Well no, I was going to school. You were in college at that time. You were in college? Yeah. And I was taking lessons from her, classical music from her. And so she said, why don't you find a part of your band? Because I came to play... She couldn't play the type of music that I played. And she realized that a lot of people at that time... You know, in the present time... You go down the street or somebody... I wish I could do that. And you know, they said, you can't do it. And then this is easy... It comes easy to you. And they couldn't do it. So this lady could not... Could not swing. She couldn't play any jazz music. So she encouraged me. She said, why don't you... She saw that I had a kind of a yin for it. She said, why don't you do it? So I said, well I believe I will. So what she did, she told me to get up to three or four fellows. And I got up to three or four fellows. And we just went along and finally we began to get rather popular. Played here and there. You were playing mostly at the college or even around town? No, I played around town. So what? We played mostly for white audiences? Anybody. Yeah, any audience. Because at the yin now... The way I see it, the attraction now is not toward Negro bands or Negro artists now. No. It's toward whites. You go to clubs. Look at the clubs now. I go, who play in the clubs? But you find no white people playing the clubs. Negro, he was an oddity then. And they invited him. Invited him to different places and all like that. And they were amazed at the way we played. Oh, I see. You see? And so we were an oddity. Oh, so you played before a lot of social white people at that time as well as Negro. Yeah, that's true. That's true. That's true. Well, did you play nice supper club type music? You didn't jazz it up too much at these films? Well, it all depends what the track it was staying. Well, were you trying to play jazz? I wouldn't make it in that. I wouldn't make it in that. It just came naturally. You were playing jazz though. Yeah, but these fellas had an influence. Harvey Twiggs. Fletcher Henderson had an influence over me. What were some of the early things that you all played? What did you have a, what was the group consistent? Do you all count? We had trumpet. We had trumpet, clarinet, bass drum, bass drum and bass violin. Well, who were these fellas? Were they in college with you? No, they were not in college with me. Do you remember any of their names? Yeah, I remember some of them. I remember this fella, let me see, he came bottom. J.C. Yeah. Yeah, he was in college. He was in high school. I knew he was from here. Yeah. Was he in your band? Yeah. J.C. Yeah. Was he on the trombone week? My goodness. I don't think anybody ever knew that before. No. He played right here with you, didn't he? That's right. And was he in the first band you had? First band. What year was this, you said? I don't know what year it was. 18? I don't know what year it was. He was around about. Just after the war. 19, 19? 19, 19, yeah. Because we played, we played for years down there on Auburn Avenue. Oh, you mean in a club? In a club. I mean, we played in a place called Roof Garden. You ever heard of that? No. Roof Garden. What kind of place was it? It was a public building, six stories. And on top of this six story, he had a dance hall on the sixth floor. Was this, you pay a dime, a taxi type thing? You'd dance, kind of like the Rose one? You paid a quarter to go in. And on the holidays, you paid 50 cents. And this, and you danced with girls there? And you took your own girl? I mean, they didn't have taxi dance. You took your own girl if you wanted to. And they, on the holidays, like what, tonight, November 11th, they would have an all-night dance. Dance start at 8.30. Well, did you alternate with another band during these all-night dances? No, one of the fellows would relieve me. They would relieve me. They just, so I took you out, I played for you for a while. Well, did you remember anything outstanding about Higginbotham at the time? Higginbotham was an unusual musician. He was, I understand, a rather moody individual. Very moody. Very moody and some-timing. And then he was off playing sometimes. He wouldn't want to work. And he just didn't feel like working. He just went on downstairs somewhere. And that's why I came back for his money and like that. But he never did like to pin down. He liked to be pinned down. He was a free agent. He didn't like a lot of routine play. No. No. He didn't like that. Well, did he have the broad, hot tone then that he had? I don't remember where he had the hot tone then, but he had a good tone more than an average person. And he was a substantial musician. That is, he always knew when his time came to come in. Because there was always a substantial beat. And always a new rhythm. And you enjoyed it.
